foundations.title: Professional Foundations — Scotland
foundations.action: Explain your SSSC role, employer and the purpose of involvement; check any specialist appointment required for the work.
foundations.record: Use an outcomes conversation to connect daily living, relationships, poverty and service barriers to an assessment. Take a conflict between resources and assessed need to supervision with evidence and a proposed response. Link continuous professional learning to feedback and a change in practice, using the current SSSC requirements. Use the employer’s complaints process for a service decision and the SSSC route for a concern about a registered worker’s fitness to practise. Explain that these address different questions. A complaint to a regulator does not automatically review a funding decision.

care-support.title: Social Care and Support — Scotland
care-support.action: Assess personal outcomes and explain which community-care duty and eligibility policy are being applied.
care-support.record: Offer and explain the four SDS options, including practical assistance with managing the chosen arrangement. Consider an adult carer support plan or young carer statement separately from the cared-for person’s assessment. Record the support budget, any charging decision, agreed provision and how unmet needs will be escalated. Ask for the authority’s written reasons and information about reconsideration or complaints when assessment, eligibility or provision is disputed. Use the current SDS and carers guidance for the particular issue. Independent advocacy and accessible information can make participation effective.

mca.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — Scotland
mca.action: Identify the decision and use communication support before concluding that the adult cannot act or decide.
mca.record: Apply the AWI principles to the proposed intervention and describe the benefit sought. Read any power of attorney or court order and check scope, activation and limits. For medical treatment, check the Part 5 certification and treatment framework with the responsible clinician; do not treat a social-work assessment as clinical authorisation. Disagreement about a proxy, treatment or a court order requires the relevant AWI route, not simply a majority vote at a meeting. The Mental Welfare Commission provides rights information; the Office of the Public Guardian and sheriff court have different functions depending on the issue.

dols.title: Restrictions and Liberty — Scotland
dols.action: Describe the actual restrictions and the person’s responses, including attempted departures and staff interventions.
dols.record: Identify whether the proposed authority is an AWI order, a mental-health measure or another lawful route. Read the exact powers and seek specialist advice where confinement or disputed authority is involved. Arrange a less restrictive plan, independent support and a named review of necessity and objections. Use the court or tribunal route appropriate to the actual measure. The Mental Welfare Commission can advise about rights and concerns. A welfare order and a compulsory mental-health order should not be described as interchangeable, and neither removes the need to review everyday restrictions.

mha.title: Mental Health — Scotland
mha.action: Identify whether emergency detention, short-term detention or an application for a compulsory treatment order is proposed.
mha.record: Map evidence to that route’s criteria, including the contribution of voluntary and community alternatives. Identify the responsible medical professionals, MHO and Mental Health Tribunal for Scotland functions. Separate psychiatric treatment safeguards from the authority for unrelated physical healthcare. Explain access to independent advocacy, the named-person arrangements that apply, legal representation and tribunal review. Particular treatments have additional safeguards. Use the Mental Welfare Commission rights guidance and the actual order when explaining the person’s position.

safeguarding.title: Adult Safeguarding — Scotland
safeguarding.action: Refer concerns on the basis of the available evidence; a referrer need not prove that all criteria are met.
safeguarding.record: Consider each criterion explicitly in council inquiries and revisit it as circumstances change. Identify the council officer’s role, partner-agency responsibilities and any need for police involvement. Apply the Act’s benefit and least restrictive principles, consider advocacy and distinguish support from compulsory powers. The 2022 Code explains participation, consent and the safeguards around investigations and protection measures. Seek the relevant legal advice before coercive action; a protection concern does not confer unlimited entry, removal or treatment powers.

children.title: Children, Families and Transitions — Scotland
children.action: Use the child’s account and daily-life evidence alongside family strengths and protection concerns.
children.record: Apply GIRFEC and current national child-protection guidance without treating a wellbeing concern as automatic compulsory authority. Identify whether local-authority support, a protection response or a referral to the Reporter is required. Plan transitions with education, health and adult services, verifying actual acceptance and continuing responsibilities. Children should receive accessible explanations and appropriate advocacy or legal support for the process affecting them. The UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Act 2024 adds duties within its statutory scope; check that scope rather than describing every public decision as covered in the same way.

rights.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — Scotland
rights.action: Identify the actual decision and the public body or service responsible for it.
rights.record: Consider equality barriers and reasonable adjustments in assessment, communication and service access. For information sharing, identify the applicable lawful basis and any additional condition for sensitive data; distinguish confidentiality from data protection. Record reasons, alternatives and disagreement, and explain the organisation’s access, correction and complaints routes. A service complaint, a data-protection complaint and a court or tribunal challenge have different purposes and timescales. Help the person identify the remedy they seek and obtain advice on the relevant route; an internal review does not necessarily preserve a separate legal deadline.

sources.title: Scotland Source Library
sources.action: Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.
sources.record: Record the exact source and provision used, date accessed and any unresolved question.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Scotland practice guide?
cards.answer: The Scottish Social Services Council (SSSC) Codes of Practice apply to workers and employers. The revised Codes took effect on 1 May 2024. Professional registration and employer procedures serve different purposes: an employer can allocate work but cannot confer a statutory appointment or qualification that a particular function requires.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Identify the responsible local authority, Health and Social Care Partnership, NHS service or voluntary organisation. Integration does not remove the need to identify who is exercising a duty, holding a record or making a funding decision. The SSSC regulates the workforce; the Care Inspectorate regulates registered care services.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Explain your SSSC role, employer and the purpose of involvement; check any specialist appointment required for the work. Use an outcomes conversation to connect daily living, relationships, poverty and service barriers to an assessment. Take a conflict between resources and assessed need to supervision with evidence and a proposed response. Link continuous professional learning to feedback and a change in practice, using the current SSSC requirements.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Use the employer’s complaints process for a service decision and the SSSC route for a concern about a registered worker’s fitness to practise. Explain that these address different questions. A complaint to a regulator does not automatically review a funding decision.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating an employer instruction as the complete explanation for a professional decision.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Scotland practice guide?
cards.answer: Community care sits across the Social Work (Scotland) Act 1968, the Social Care (Self-directed Support) (Scotland) Act 2013 and the Carers (Scotland) Act 2016. Identify the relevant assessment duty and local eligibility policy. A budget calculation is a different step from identifying the person’s needs.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The 2025 statutory SDS guidance describes four options: a direct payment; support selected by the person and arranged through the authority or an agreed third party; support selected and arranged by the authority with the person; or a combination. Discuss the choices rather than treating one option as the default.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Assess personal outcomes and explain which community-care duty and eligibility policy are being applied. Offer and explain the four SDS options, including practical assistance with managing the chosen arrangement. Consider an adult carer support plan or young carer statement separately from the cared-for person’s assessment. Record the support budget, any charging decision, agreed provision and how unmet needs will be escalated.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Ask for the authority’s written reasons and information about reconsideration or complaints when assessment, eligibility or provision is disputed. Use the current SDS and carers guidance for the particular issue. Independent advocacy and accessible information can make participation effective.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Presenting SDS as direct payments only, or treating a relative’s preference as the adult’s choice.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Scotland practice guide?
cards.answer: The Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 (AWI) provides different routes for welfare, property and treatment decisions. Its principles require benefit that cannot reasonably be achieved without intervention, the least restrictive option, attention to the adult’s wishes, consultation with relevant people, and encouragement of the adult’s skills.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: For the matter in question, AWI incapacity concerns inability to act, decide, communicate or understand a decision, or remember it, because of mental disorder or inability to communicate caused by physical disability. A communication difficulty that human or mechanical assistance can resolve does not itself satisfy the definition. A welfare attorney, guardian or person holding an intervention order has only the powers actually conferred. A financial appointment does not provide general welfare authority.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the decision and use communication support before concluding that the adult cannot act or decide. Apply the AWI principles to the proposed intervention and describe the benefit sought. Read any power of attorney or court order and check scope, activation and limits. For medical treatment, check the Part 5 certification and treatment framework with the responsible clinician; do not treat a social-work assessment as clinical authorisation.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Disagreement about a proxy, treatment or a court order requires the relevant AWI route, not simply a majority vote at a meeting. The Mental Welfare Commission provides rights information; the Office of the Public Guardian and sheriff court have different functions depending on the issue.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Using a global incapacity label or assuming that any attorney can make every decision.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Scotland practice guide?
cards.answer: Scottish restrictions require analysis under the applicable welfare, mental-health and human-rights framework. There is no English hospital/care-home authorisation scheme to copy. AWI welfare guardianship or an intervention order may be relevant, but the wording and lawful scope of a particular order matter.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Distinguish agreement to support, authority for a welfare decision and the legal justification for actual confinement. Where arrangements may engage Article 5, obtain current advice about the applicable legal test and route. A service’s description of a placement as voluntary does not resolve what happens if the person wants to leave.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Describe the actual restrictions and the person’s responses, including attempted departures and staff interventions. Identify whether the proposed authority is an AWI order, a mental-health measure or another lawful route. Read the exact powers and seek specialist advice where confinement or disputed authority is involved. Arrange a less restrictive plan, independent support and a named review of necessity and objections.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Use the court or tribunal route appropriate to the actual measure. The Mental Welfare Commission can advise about rights and concerns. A welfare order and a compulsory mental-health order should not be described as interchangeable, and neither removes the need to review everyday restrictions.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming that guardianship automatically authorises every restriction used by a provider.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Scotland practice guide?
cards.answer: The Mental Health (Care and Treatment) (Scotland) Act 2003 provides emergency, short-term and longer-term compulsory routes, with amendments including the Mental Health (Scotland) Act 2015. A Mental Health Officer (MHO) has a specific statutory role; being a social worker does not itself confer that appointment.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: For a compulsory treatment order, the criteria concern mental disorder, available treatment, significant risk without treatment, significantly impaired decision-making ability about medical treatment because of the disorder, and necessity. The exact criteria differ between routes. Significantly impaired decision-making ability is not simply another name for the AWI incapacity test.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify whether emergency detention, short-term detention or an application for a compulsory treatment order is proposed. Map evidence to that route’s criteria, including the contribution of voluntary and community alternatives. Identify the responsible medical professionals, MHO and Mental Health Tribunal for Scotland functions. Separate psychiatric treatment safeguards from the authority for unrelated physical healthcare.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain access to independent advocacy, the named-person arrangements that apply, legal representation and tribunal review. Particular treatments have additional safeguards. Use the Mental Welfare Commission rights guidance and the actual order when explaining the person’s position.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Using one detention threshold for every route, or equating refusal with the statutory decision-making criterion.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Scotland practice guide?
cards.answer: The Adult Support and Protection (Scotland) Act 2007 concerns adults aged 16 or over meeting all three criteria: inability to safeguard their own wellbeing, property, rights or interests; risk of harm; and greater vulnerability to harm because of disability, mental disorder, illness or physical or mental infirmity. Capacity is not a separate gateway requirement.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The council’s inquiry duty, investigative powers and protection orders are distinct. The three criteria are not an eligibility test for ordinary support. A finding that this Act is not the appropriate route should lead to consideration of other available help, rather than automatic case closure.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Refer concerns on the basis of the available evidence; a referrer need not prove that all criteria are met. Consider each criterion explicitly in council inquiries and revisit it as circumstances change. Identify the council officer’s role, partner-agency responsibilities and any need for police involvement. Apply the Act’s benefit and least restrictive principles, consider advocacy and distinguish support from compulsory powers.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The 2022 Code explains participation, consent and the safeguards around investigations and protection measures. Seek the relevant legal advice before coercive action; a protection concern does not confer unlimited entry, removal or treatment powers.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating capacity as proof that an adult can protect themselves, or using protection criteria to deny ordinary services.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Scotland practice guide?
cards.answer: The Children (Scotland) Act 1995 and Children’s Hearings (Scotland) Act 2011 provide important duties and compulsory-measure routes. GIRFEC is the national practice framework for coordinated support. Its SHANARRI wellbeing indicators organise enquiry; they do not replace the legal grounds and safeguards for a compulsory measure.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: A child’s plan and a lead professional can coordinate services. Referral to the Children’s Reporter and decisions in the hearings system are separate from an ordinary support meeting. Explain which process is being used, why, and how the child and family can participate.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Use the child’s account and daily-life evidence alongside family strengths and protection concerns. Apply GIRFEC and current national child-protection guidance without treating a wellbeing concern as automatic compulsory authority. Identify whether local-authority support, a protection response or a referral to the Reporter is required. Plan transitions with education, health and adult services, verifying actual acceptance and continuing responsibilities.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Children should receive accessible explanations and appropriate advocacy or legal support for the process affecting them. The UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Act 2024 adds duties within its statutory scope; check that scope rather than describing every public decision as covered in the same way.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating GIRFEC as a power to compel cooperation or assuming adult support will begin automatically at transition.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Scotland practice guide?
cards.answer: Scottish practice engages the Human Rights Act 1998, Equality Act 2010 and the applicable UK data-protection framework, alongside local statutory duties. The SSSC Codes provide professional expectations; they do not replace the legal basis for an intervention or disclosure.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Act 2024 strengthens children’s rights within its defined scope. Identify the source of the public function and the statutory limits before asserting that a particular action breaches its compatibility duty. Participation and accessible explanations remain essential to a reasoned assessment.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the actual decision and the public body or service responsible for it. Consider equality barriers and reasonable adjustments in assessment, communication and service access. For information sharing, identify the applicable lawful basis and any additional condition for sensitive data; distinguish confidentiality from data protection. Record reasons, alternatives and disagreement, and explain the organisation’s access, correction and complaints routes.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: A service complaint, a data-protection complaint and a court or tribunal challenge have different purposes and timescales. Help the person identify the remedy they seek and obtain advice on the relevant route; an internal review does not necessarily preserve a separate legal deadline.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Writing that equality was considered without identifying the barrier, adjustment or effect on the decision.

The professional body identified for this guide. Check its remit and the requirements that apply to your role.
Support to express views, understand choices and participate; statutory entitlements depend on the local framework.
Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.
Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.
Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.
The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.
Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.
Someone with a defined support or decision-making role; verify the source and scope of authority.
A reasoned comparison of intended benefit, burdens, rights and alternatives.
Attention to power, identity and the person’s experience of a service, informed by their preferences.
Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.
Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.
Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.
Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.
A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.
Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.
Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.
An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.
A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.
An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

theoryLenses.title: Ecological Systems Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.
test: What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

theoryLenses.title: Strengths-Based Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.
test: What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

theoryLenses.title: Trauma-Informed Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.
test: What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

theoryLenses.title: Attachment Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.
test: How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

theoryLenses.title: Systems and Family Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.
test: Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

theoryLenses.title: Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.
test: What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

theoryLenses.title: Crisis Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.
test: What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

theoryLenses.title: Life Course Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.
test: What transitions or losses are happening now?
How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

theoryLenses.title: Task-Centred Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.
test: What problem does the person most want to work on first?
What is the smallest useful next step?
Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

hypothesisSignals.label: Self-neglect, hoarding, home conditions, or repeated crisis presentations.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Think about trauma, executive functioning, environment, identity, isolation, loss, and safeguarding thresholds.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person appears to refuse support, miss visits, or disengage.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Avoid jumping straight to non-compliance. Consider trust, trauma, power, communication, and whether the offer fits the person.

hypothesisSignals.label: Family conflict, carer strain, coercion, or unclear roles are present.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Map roles, power, risk, protective factors, and what happens when professionals intervene.

hypothesisSignals.label: Risk has escalated quickly or a crisis is dominating the assessment.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Separate immediate stabilisation from longer-term formulation and legal route decisions.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is a transition: adolescence to adulthood, hospital discharge, bereavement, moving home, or ageing.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Transitions can disrupt identity, support, eligibility, relationships, and coping.

hypothesisSignals.label: Discrimination, poverty, inaccessible services, stigma, or cultural misunderstanding may be relevant.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Test whether systems are creating or worsening the difficulty.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person or carer feels overwhelmed and cannot see a way forward.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Consider crisis, small steps, stabilisation, advocacy, and practical environmental change.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is mistrust of professionals, fear of services, or repeated complaints.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Explore previous experiences, power, communication, consistency, and whether the person has reason to feel unsafe.

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Safety
childPracticeModels.use: Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What are we worried about, what is working well, and what needs to happen for the child to be safe enough?
test: Can worries be written in plain language that the family understands?
What existing safety has been demonstrated, not just promised?
Who is in the family network and what role can they safely take?

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging
childPracticeModels.use: Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What would wellbeing, safety, permanence, connection, and belonging look like from the child's perspective?
test: What does the child say or show about where they feel safe and connected?
What would meaningful stability look like in daily life?
How are family relationships, identity, culture, and belonging being protected?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Whole-family child protection where parental domestic abuse, mental health, substance misuse, trauma, or adult needs affect child safety.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety may improve when adult needs and risks are addressed alongside direct work with the child and family network.
test: Which adult needs are directly affecting child safety or care?
Is the plan joined up across children's and adults' services?
Are adult-focused interventions linked to measurable child safety outcomes?

childPracticeModels.title: Contextual Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Harm may be located outside the home, in peer, school, community, or online contexts that parents cannot control alone.
test: Where is harm happening: home, school, peer group, community, online, or transport?
Which context needs intervention, not only which child or parent?
Who has power or influence in that context?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Group Conferencing
childPracticeModels.use: Family-led planning, kinship care, safety planning, pre-proceedings, reunification, and support network building.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The wider family network may hold safe, practical solutions that have not yet been fully mapped or invited in.
test: Who does the child identify as family or trusted network?
What information does the family need before private planning?
How will the plan be checked for safety, clarity, and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Systemic Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Family patterns, repeated cycles, communication, roles, meaning, conflict, and relationship-based formulation.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The concern may be maintained by family patterns, relationship roles, service responses, or repeated cycles.
test: What pattern repeats, and what keeps it going?
How does each person make sense of the problem?
What would change if one part of the system responded differently?

childPracticeModels.title: Motivational Interviewing
childPracticeModels.use: Ambivalence, parental engagement, adolescent risk, substance use, resistance, and behaviour change conversations.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The parent or young person may be caught between reasons to change and reasons to keep things as they are.
test: What does the person want to be different?
What are their reasons for change and reasons against change?
Are we arguing for change so hard that the person argues against it?

childPracticeModels.title: Solution-Focused Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Goal-setting, exceptions, scaling, strengths, future-focused planning, and building on small signs of progress.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Small exceptions or signs of safety may reveal what can be repeated, strengthened, and built into the plan.
test: When is the problem slightly less serious?
What would one point higher on the safety scale look like?
What has the family already done that helped, even briefly?

childPracticeModels.title: PACE and DDP-Informed Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The child may need relational safety through playfulness, acceptance, curiosity, and empathy before they can reflect or change.
test: How does the child's behaviour make sense as communication or protection?
How can adults stay curious without shaming or escalating?
What helps the child experience safety in the relationship?

childPracticeModels.title: Safe and Together
childPracticeModels.use: Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety work should focus on the perpetrator's pattern of behaviour and avoid blaming the non-abusive parent for the abuse.
test: What is the perpetrator's pattern and impact on the child?
What has the protective parent done to promote safety?
Does the plan increase accountability for the person causing harm?

childPracticeModels.title: Graded Care Profile 2
childPracticeModels.use: Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The quality of care may need structured, observable mapping rather than vague descriptions of neglect.
test: Which care domains are strong, inconsistent, or harmful?
What evidence has been observed rather than assumed?
Is change measurable across time and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Restorative Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Progress may come through relationship repair, accountability, and shared planning rather than only professional direction.
test: Who has been affected and what do they need?
What repair or accountability is realistic and safe?
How will the meeting avoid blame and keep the child central?

childModelSignals.label: Child protection concerns, safety planning, or danger statements are needed.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs clear worries, existing safety, safety goals, family network planning, and review.

childModelSignals.label: Neglect, home conditions, missed health needs, or inconsistent care are central.
childModelSignals.detail: The assessment needs observable evidence, care domains, impact on the child, and change over time.

childModelSignals.label: Domestic abuse is affecting the child or family safety.
childModelSignals.detail: The plan needs perpetrator pattern analysis, protective parent strengths, child impact, and safe information sharing.

childModelSignals.label: Exploitation, adolescent risk, peer harm, school risk, or online/community harm is present.
childModelSignals.detail: Risk may sit outside the home and require contextual mapping beyond parent-focused plans.

childModelSignals.label: The child is in care, on the edge of care, returning home, or permanence is uncertain.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs belonging, stability, identity, relationships, family network options, and safe permanence planning.

childModelSignals.label: Trauma, attachment disruption, mistrust, shame, or relational conflict is central.
childModelSignals.detail: The child may need relational safety and adults who can stay curious, calm, boundaried, and empathic.

childModelSignals.label: There may be wider family or trusted network members who could help.
childModelSignals.detail: The network may hold safe options for care, practical support, supervision, or belonging.

childModelSignals.label: A parent or young person feels ambivalent, defensive, stuck, or hard to engage.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs careful engagement, change talk, respect for autonomy, and clarity about non-negotiable safety.

childModelSignals.label: There has been conflict, harm, school exclusion, relationship breakdown, or a need for repair.
childModelSignals.detail: The work may need accountability, safe dialogue, relationship repair, and a shared plan.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Professional Foundations — Scotland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A worker is asked to close a referral because a family has missed two appointments. The person says bus fares and caring duties prevented attendance.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Test the access barrier before concluding that support is unwanted. Offer a workable contact method, clarify the person’s outcomes and record the referral decision and its reasons. In supervision, distinguish a resource pressure from evidence about need and willingness.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Social Care and Support — Scotland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An adult wants assistance to attend evening activities, while a parent asks the authority to arrange all daytime support.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Explore the adult’s outcomes and whether a combination of SDS options would fit. Establish what the parent is willing to do and any need for a separate carer plan. Confirm actual evening provision, management support and costs before describing the package as agreed.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — Scotland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A man can choose his meals and visitors but struggles to understand a proposed sale of his home. His sister holds a welfare power of attorney.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Keep the property decision distinct from daily choices and welfare matters. Provide accessible financial information and check the document’s powers. Do not let the welfare appointment stand in for financial authority. Explain which advice or court process is needed if the sale remains necessary and authority is missing.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Restrictions and Liberty — Scotland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A supported-living service locks the front door at night and says a guardian agreed to the placement. The adult repeatedly asks to leave.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Obtain the order and distinguish placement powers from the measures staff enforce. Record the adult’s wishes, actual ability to leave and alternatives such as staffing or environmental changes. Escalate the legal basis of confinement promptly and arrange support to challenge it; family approval is insufficient reasoning.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Mental Health — Scotland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A person experiencing severe mental distress declines admission but accepts daily support and an urgent medical review at home.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Assess whether the proposed community support is real and sufficient, and compare it with the relevant statutory criteria. Record the person’s reasoning and the MHO’s assessment. Do not substitute disagreement with the recommended treatment for evidence of significantly impaired decision-making ability or necessity.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Adult Safeguarding — Scotland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A 61-year-old understands their bank account but depends on a neighbour who takes their money and controls access to shopping.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Do not reject the concern because the adult can explain the transactions. Explore dependency, coercion and ability to safeguard their interests against the three criteria. Arrange a safe conversation, practical access to essentials and the appropriate council and police response.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Children, Families and Transitions — Scotland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A 15-year-old misses school to support an ill parent and says they want to stay at home but need help.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Explore the young person’s safety, education and caring responsibilities. Coordinate support and consider a young carer statement. Establish whether there is evidence requiring a protection or Reporter route, while avoiding a conclusion that school absence alone settles that question.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — Scotland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A deaf parent is offered only telephone appointments and is then described as failing to engage with a family assessment.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Arrange suitable communication support, correct the inaccurate inference and reassess the effect of the service barrier. Record the parent’s preferred method, the adjustment agreed and responsibility for providing it. Review the assessment outcome in light of the earlier exclusion.

printableTemplates.title: Professional Foundations
printableTemplates.summary: Explain your professional role, distinguish an ethical concern from a statutory power, and turn a formulation into an accountable plan.
printableTemplates.body:
Professional Foundations
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Scottish Social Services Council (SSSC) Codes of Practice apply to workers and employers. The revised Codes took effect on 1 May 2024. Professional registration and employer procedures serve different purposes: an employer can allocate work but cannot confer a statutory appointment or qualification that a particular function requires.

Identify the responsible local authority, Health and Social Care Partnership, NHS service or voluntary organisation. Integration does not remove the need to identify who is exercising a duty, holding a record or making a funding decision. The SSSC regulates the workforce; the Care Inspectorate regulates registered care services.

Local pathway:
Explain your SSSC role, employer and the purpose of involvement; check any specialist appointment required for the work.
Use an outcomes conversation to connect daily living, relationships, poverty and service barriers to an assessment.
Take a conflict between resources and assessed need to supervision with evidence and a proposed response.
Link continuous professional learning to feedback and a change in practice, using the current SSSC requirements.

Recording prompts:
1. Your role and the legal or professional framework
Notes:

2. The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
Notes:

3. Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
Notes:

4. Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
Notes:

5. Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Use the employer’s complaints process for a service decision and the SSSC route for a concern about a registered worker’s fitness to practise. Explain that these address different questions. A complaint to a regulator does not automatically review a funding decision.

Sources:
https://www.sssc.uk.com/standards/codes-of-practice/

printableTemplates.title: Social Care and Support
printableTemplates.summary: Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.
printableTemplates.body:
Social Care and Support
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Community care sits across the Social Work (Scotland) Act 1968, the Social Care (Self-directed Support) (Scotland) Act 2013 and the Carers (Scotland) Act 2016. Identify the relevant assessment duty and local eligibility policy. A budget calculation is a different step from identifying the person’s needs.

The 2025 statutory SDS guidance describes four options: a direct payment; support selected by the person and arranged through the authority or an agreed third party; support selected and arranged by the authority with the person; or a combination. Discuss the choices rather than treating one option as the default.

Local pathway:
Assess personal outcomes and explain which community-care duty and eligibility policy are being applied.
Offer and explain the four SDS options, including practical assistance with managing the chosen arrangement.
Consider an adult carer support plan or young carer statement separately from the cared-for person’s assessment.
Record the support budget, any charging decision, agreed provision and how unmet needs will be escalated.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Ask for the authority’s written reasons and information about reconsideration or complaints when assessment, eligibility or provision is disputed. Use the current SDS and carers guidance for the particular issue. Independent advocacy and accessible information can make participation effective.

Sources:
https://www.gov.scot/publications/statutory-guidance-accompany-social-care-self-directed-support-scotland-act-2013-updated-2025/
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2013/1/contents
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2016/9/contents

printableTemplates.title: Decision-Making and Capacity
printableTemplates.summary: Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.
printableTemplates.body:
Decision-Making and Capacity
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 (AWI) provides different routes for welfare, property and treatment decisions. Its principles require benefit that cannot reasonably be achieved without intervention, the least restrictive option, attention to the adult’s wishes, consultation with relevant people, and encouragement of the adult’s skills.

For the matter in question, AWI incapacity concerns inability to act, decide, communicate or understand a decision, or remember it, because of mental disorder or inability to communicate caused by physical disability. A communication difficulty that human or mechanical assistance can resolve does not itself satisfy the definition. A welfare attorney, guardian or person holding an intervention order has only the powers actually conferred. A financial appointment does not provide general welfare authority.

Local pathway:
Identify the decision and use communication support before concluding that the adult cannot act or decide.
Apply the AWI principles to the proposed intervention and describe the benefit sought.
Read any power of attorney or court order and check scope, activation and limits.
For medical treatment, check the Part 5 certification and treatment framework with the responsible clinician; do not treat a social-work assessment as clinical authorisation.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Disagreement about a proxy, treatment or a court order requires the relevant AWI route, not simply a majority vote at a meeting. The Mental Welfare Commission provides rights information; the Office of the Public Guardian and sheriff court have different functions depending on the issue.

Sources:
https://www.gov.scot/publications/adults-with-incapacity-act-principles/
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2000/4/contents
https://www.mwcscot.org.uk/looking-help/your-rights

printableTemplates.title: Restrictions and Liberty
printableTemplates.summary: Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.
printableTemplates.body:
Restrictions and Liberty
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Scottish restrictions require analysis under the applicable welfare, mental-health and human-rights framework. There is no English hospital/care-home authorisation scheme to copy. AWI welfare guardianship or an intervention order may be relevant, but the wording and lawful scope of a particular order matter.

Distinguish agreement to support, authority for a welfare decision and the legal justification for actual confinement. Where arrangements may engage Article 5, obtain current advice about the applicable legal test and route. A service’s description of a placement as voluntary does not resolve what happens if the person wants to leave.

Local pathway:
Describe the actual restrictions and the person’s responses, including attempted departures and staff interventions.
Identify whether the proposed authority is an AWI order, a mental-health measure or another lawful route.
Read the exact powers and seek specialist advice where confinement or disputed authority is involved.
Arrange a less restrictive plan, independent support and a named review of necessity and objections.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Use the court or tribunal route appropriate to the actual measure. The Mental Welfare Commission can advise about rights and concerns. A welfare order and a compulsory mental-health order should not be described as interchangeable, and neither removes the need to review everyday restrictions.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2000/4/contents
https://www.mwcscot.org.uk/looking-help/your-rights

printableTemplates.title: Mental Health
printableTemplates.summary: Distinguish voluntary care, compulsory assessment, detention and treatment; connect the local criteria to evidence and explain the person’s review rights.
printableTemplates.body:
Mental Health
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Health (Care and Treatment) (Scotland) Act 2003 provides emergency, short-term and longer-term compulsory routes, with amendments including the Mental Health (Scotland) Act 2015. A Mental Health Officer (MHO) has a specific statutory role; being a social worker does not itself confer that appointment.

For a compulsory treatment order, the criteria concern mental disorder, available treatment, significant risk without treatment, significantly impaired decision-making ability about medical treatment because of the disorder, and necessity. The exact criteria differ between routes. Significantly impaired decision-making ability is not simply another name for the AWI incapacity test.

Local pathway:
Identify whether emergency detention, short-term detention or an application for a compulsory treatment order is proposed.
Map evidence to that route’s criteria, including the contribution of voluntary and community alternatives.
Identify the responsible medical professionals, MHO and Mental Health Tribunal for Scotland functions.
Separate psychiatric treatment safeguards from the authority for unrelated physical healthcare.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain access to independent advocacy, the named-person arrangements that apply, legal representation and tribunal review. Particular treatments have additional safeguards. Use the Mental Welfare Commission rights guidance and the actual order when explaining the person’s position.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2003/13/contents
https://www.mwcscot.org.uk/looking-help/your-rights
https://www.mwcscot.org.uk/node/510

printableTemplates.title: Adult Safeguarding
printableTemplates.summary: Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.
printableTemplates.body:
Adult Safeguarding
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Adult Support and Protection (Scotland) Act 2007 concerns adults aged 16 or over meeting all three criteria: inability to safeguard their own wellbeing, property, rights or interests; risk of harm; and greater vulnerability to harm because of disability, mental disorder, illness or physical or mental infirmity. Capacity is not a separate gateway requirement.

The council’s inquiry duty, investigative powers and protection orders are distinct. The three criteria are not an eligibility test for ordinary support. A finding that this Act is not the appropriate route should lead to consideration of other available help, rather than automatic case closure.

Local pathway:
Refer concerns on the basis of the available evidence; a referrer need not prove that all criteria are met.
Consider each criterion explicitly in council inquiries and revisit it as circumstances change.
Identify the council officer’s role, partner-agency responsibilities and any need for police involvement.
Apply the Act’s benefit and least restrictive principles, consider advocacy and distinguish support from compulsory powers.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The 2022 Code explains participation, consent and the safeguards around investigations and protection measures. Seek the relevant legal advice before coercive action; a protection concern does not confer unlimited entry, removal or treatment powers.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2007/10/contents
https://www.gov.scot/publications/adult-support-protection-scotland-act-2007-guidance-general-practice/pages/2/

printableTemplates.title: Children, Families and Transitions
printableTemplates.summary: Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.
printableTemplates.body:
Children, Families and Transitions
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Children (Scotland) Act 1995 and Children’s Hearings (Scotland) Act 2011 provide important duties and compulsory-measure routes. GIRFEC is the national practice framework for coordinated support. Its SHANARRI wellbeing indicators organise enquiry; they do not replace the legal grounds and safeguards for a compulsory measure.

A child’s plan and a lead professional can coordinate services. Referral to the Children’s Reporter and decisions in the hearings system are separate from an ordinary support meeting. Explain which process is being used, why, and how the child and family can participate.

Local pathway:
Use the child’s account and daily-life evidence alongside family strengths and protection concerns.
Apply GIRFEC and current national child-protection guidance without treating a wellbeing concern as automatic compulsory authority.
Identify whether local-authority support, a protection response or a referral to the Reporter is required.
Plan transitions with education, health and adult services, verifying actual acceptance and continuing responsibilities.

Recording prompts:
1. Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
Notes:

2. Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
Notes:

3. Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
Notes:

4. Family participation, culture and legal authority
Notes:

5. Named plan, education/health links and transition dates
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Children should receive accessible explanations and appropriate advocacy or legal support for the process affecting them. The UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Act 2024 adds duties within its statutory scope; check that scope rather than describing every public decision as covered in the same way.

Sources:
https://www.gov.scot/policies/girfec/
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1995/36/contents
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2011/1/contents

printableTemplates.title: Rights, Culture and Recording
printableTemplates.summary: Connect rights to an actual service decision, distinguish privacy from absolute secrecy and write a record that makes reasons and disagreement visible.
printableTemplates.body:
Rights, Culture and Recording
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Scottish practice engages the Human Rights Act 1998, Equality Act 2010 and the applicable UK data-protection framework, alongside local statutory duties. The SSSC Codes provide professional expectations; they do not replace the legal basis for an intervention or disclosure.

The UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Act 2024 strengthens children’s rights within its defined scope. Identify the source of the public function and the statutory limits before asserting that a particular action breaches its compatibility duty. Participation and accessible explanations remain essential to a reasoned assessment.

Local pathway:
Identify the actual decision and the public body or service responsible for it.
Consider equality barriers and reasonable adjustments in assessment, communication and service access.
For information sharing, identify the applicable lawful basis and any additional condition for sensitive data; distinguish confidentiality from data protection.
Record reasons, alternatives and disagreement, and explain the organisation’s access, correction and complaints routes.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
Notes:

2. Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
Notes:

3. Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
Notes:

4. Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
Notes:

5. Access, correction, complaints and review route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
A service complaint, a data-protection complaint and a court or tribunal challenge have different purposes and timescales. Help the person identify the remedy they seek and obtain advice on the relevant route; an internal review does not necessarily preserve a separate legal deadline.

Sources:
https://www.gov.scot/policies/human-rights/childrens-rights/
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2010/15/contents
https://www.sssc.uk.com/standards/codes-of-practice/
